1.pericope_label: My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments: for length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee. Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart: so shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man

schools.summary: Henry reads the opening as a lesson in communion with God: the law is to be fixed as our rule, learned, since we cannot forget what we never knew, and remembered so as to be ready when needed; the wills and affections must conform as well as the head, and both tables of the law are to be deposited in the heart as in the ark of the testimony. He takes the promise as long life and prosperity together, the commandments adding length of days on earth and eternal life in heaven.

Gill reads my law as doctrine, the doctrine of Christ and the truths of the Gospel, too weighty to be let slip; he observes that the law of Moses promised long life to its observers while the Gospel brings immortal life to light. On mercy and truth he takes both as duties, mercy shown by relieving want, by pity and counsel, by forgiving offences and restoring the backslidden in meekness, and truth by exercising faith, speaking truth to a neighbour and holding fast the Gospel, but reports that many read the clause instead as a promise, that mercy and truth shall not forsake thee, meaning the mercy and truth of God. The favour he takes both as grace from God, as Noah found, and as esteem among men, as Joseph had with Potiphar and the keeper of the prison.

Clarke counts three eminent blessings in the promise, long days, years of lives and peace, glossed as health, long life and abundance; he asks that mercy and truth be constant companions, kept in view and made the moving principles, felt as well as seen; and he divides the favour into acceptance with God with a sense of his approbation, and a public verdict in which men weigh a character and give credit for sincerity, adding that a benevolent character is generally prized where it is well known and that the envy of men is itself a proof of the excellence of what they envy. Wesley keeps my law the law of God, called his law as the gospel is called Paul’s gospel because delivered by him, divides mercy and truth by object into benignity and charity on one side and the duties of justice on the other, has them bound like a chain with which people adorn the neck, and keeps understanding practical, the knowledge of duty and the discerning of good from evil.

Ellicott distinguishes the two terms of the promise, long life meaning a life worth living, fit to be called life, while length of days implies only extension, the reward promised for obedience to parents. He would render mercy and truth as love and faithfulness, attributes shown by God to man and by man to God and his fellow, the special attributes by which God is known in his dealings with men and therefore to be imitated; he compares the binding and writing with the figurative orders about keeping the Law whose literal interpretation produced prayer-fillets and phylacteries, corrects table to tablet, and notes that favour and good understanding are particularly used of the childhood of our Lord. Keil and Delitzsch take the neck ornament for the signet carried on a string rather than a ring, find the phylacteries in view as the external form of what is here a figure of the inward parts, and explain the tablet as one prepared for writing by polish, so that writing love and fidelity there means impressing both duties deeply enough to impel a man from within outward.

debates: Is my law the law of God or the doctrine of Christ? Gill reads it as Gospel doctrine; Wesley keeps it the law of God, called his law because delivered by him.

Are mercy and truth duties or promises? Gill takes them as duties but reports the reading that makes them the mercy and truth of God, which shall not forsake the obedient; Ellicott and Wesley treat them throughout as things required of a man.

What is added by the promise? Clarke counts three distinct blessings including prosperity; Ellicott separates a life worth living from the mere extension of days; Gill and Henry both carry the promise past this life into the next.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch identify the neck ornament as a signet carried on a string, not a ring, and read the tablet of the heart as a polished writing surface.
Ellicott traces the literal reading of the binding to the use of prayer-fillets and phylacteries, texts enclosed in a leather case and tied on at prayer.
Clarke argues that the envy of men is itself a proof of the excellence of what they envy.
themes: a law kept in the affections
length of days and a life worth living
mercy and truth as duty or as gift
a signet worn at the neck
favour with God and standing among men

5.pericope_label: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the Lord, and depart from evil. It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones

schools.summary: Henry warns that there is no greater enemy to the power of religion and the fear of God in the heart than conceitedness of our own wisdom, since those with an opinion of their own sufficiency think it a disparagement to be hampered by the rules of religion; to fear the Lord so as to depart from evil is true wisdom, but self-denyingly so. He reads the promise as serviceable even to the outward man, the prudence, temperance and sobriety religion teaches, with the good government of the appetites, tending not only to the health of the soul but to a good habit of body.

Gill defines the trust by what it excludes, not the best creature nor any creature enjoyment, not riches or strength or wisdom, not descent or education, not a man’s own deceitful heart, not works of righteousness, not a profession of religion or its duties, not frames or graces, not even faith itself, but the Lord only and at all times. To acknowledge him in all thy ways is to set him always in view, take no step without his leave, make the Scriptures counsellors, submit when things go cross and give the glory when they succeed. The conceited man, he says, will not consult others and thinks himself wiser than his teachers and than the Scriptures, wise above what is written, glorying in an acquisition he does not ascribe to God, though what men are conceited of is generally folly. On the navel he takes the knot of the intestines to stand for the inward parts and so for the whole body, notes that the Septuagint renders it simply thy body, and reports the reading that makes wisdom the subject of the promise.

Clarke lays the precept out in steps, God being the fountain of all good who has made his creatures dependent, requires them to be conscious of it, has promised to supply their need and commands them to believe without doubt; lean not, he says, means do not prop thyself, and he who trusts in his own heart is a fool. He asks that every work be begun, continued and ended with God, since we never honour him without serving ourselves, quotes an old manuscript Bible rendering of the verses, and calls self-sufficiency the ruin of mankind ever since the fall of Adam, the grand sin of the race being the endeavour to live independently of God. On the navel he refuses any more delicate meaning, since the unborn child receives all its nourishment by the umbilical cord and nothing by the mouth, and makes trust in God as necessary to nourish the soul as the cord is to a child in the womb. Wesley reads the one kind of carnal confidence as standing for every other, in bodily strength or wealth or friends, and glosses the navel as the body and the marrow as the strength of the bones.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the admonition is interposed here, since kindness and truth were commended toward God as well as men, and hold that true prosperity comes from God alone, who knows the right way to the right ends and what benefits us and can free us from what harms. They trace the word for navel to a root meaning to bind fast, making it properly the umbilical cord, cut at birth, the firm centre with which independent bodily existence begins, and reject the conjectural reading to thy flesh by which the old versions generalized the expression. Ellicott takes the navel as the centre and most important part of the body, compares the epithet given to Delphi as navel of the earth, renders marrow literally as watering or refreshing, and notes that Job reached the same result in his inquiry after wisdom.

debates: What does leaning on your own understanding mean in practice? Clarke makes it propping oneself instead of God; Wesley extends the one kind of carnal confidence to wealth, strength and friends; Gill turns it into a list of religious supports that are equally not God, down to faith itself.

Is the navel a euphemism or the thing itself? Clarke insists on the literal navel and builds his doctrine on the umbilical cord; Keil and Delitzsch agree from the root and reject the versions that generalized it to the flesh; Gill and Wesley treat it as a part standing for the whole body.

Is the promised health of body or of soul? Gill and Henry take it both ways, Henry through the temperance religion teaches; Clarke makes the bodily image entirely a figure of grace nourishing the soul.
outliers: Clarke quotes an old manuscript Bible rendering of these verses and calls self-sufficiency the ruin of mankind since the fall of Adam.
Ellicott compares the navel of the body with the epithet given to Delphi as navel of the earth.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the umbilical cord is cut at birth, so that the navel marks where independent bodily existence begins.
themes: a trust that excludes even faith itself
every work begun and ended with God
conceit as the enemy of religion
the navel taken literally
marrow read as watering

9.pericope_label: Honour the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: so shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine. My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: for whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth

schools.summary: Gill insists the gift be a man’s own, cites the Septuagint reading out of thy just labours as excluding what is got by fraud, and holds that only a proportionate part is asked; substance is the mammon of the Targum, which set against heavenly things has no substance in it, and men honour God with it by giving to the poor, especially poor saints, by supporting worship and the credit of religion, and by communicating to the ministers of the Gospel. He reads the promised plenty as bread for the eater and seed for the sower, so that givers are gainers. He also thinks the turn to chastening is placed here to forestall the objection that the children of God are often afflicted, and takes the quotation of these words in the New Testament as an exhortation spoken to children to settle the address, since my son means neither a son of Solomon according to the flesh nor those who came to him for instruction but all the children of God in every age; the chastening springs from love, with no abatement of love in it.

Clarke keeps the old gratitude-offering in force as an obligation without end, holding that a portion of the produce of everything by which we get our support belongs to God or to the poor, the representatives of Christ, in kind or in money, so that when the portion is disposed of the rest is sanctified and when it is withheld the curse lies on the whole. On chastening he unfolds the word as correction, discipline and instruction together, teaching showing the way, discipline making the teaching effectual and correction bringing the mind into a submission without which it cannot acquire knowledge; rebellion is useless, since a man who kicks against the pricks only wounds his own soul and God will either end him or mend him. He adds that the Septuagint rendering of the last clause, chasteneth every son whom he receiveth, is what the apostle quotes word for word. Wesley makes the first command a rule of expenditure, an estate laid out not to please oneself but to glorify God, the firstfruits being the chief or best, notes that this is not the way to diminish an estate but to increase it, and marks the two ways of failing under correction, making light of it and growing weary of it.

Keil and Delitzsch are surprised that the wisdom writing, separated from the ceremonial law, should commend tithes, and answer that the consciousness of the duty is older than the law of Moses, so that the words stand as a general ethical expression, the technical terms for tithing never occurring in the book; they note that the verb translated honour means to make heavy or treat as weighty while the noun for wealth properly means lightness in the sense of opulence, and identify the granary and the vat into which the must flows from the press. On the chastening they set the contrast structurally, that as God should not be forgotten in prosperity so a man should not let adversity estrange him, translate the noun as school since the verb means to take one into school, and call the pair of verses the most suitable motto for the book of Job, the first stating its problem and the second its solution. Ellicott calls the presses vats into which the newly pressed juice flowed, and reads the chastening as a wonderful advance beyond the Pentateuch, where reward and punishment followed immediately on behaviour so that misfortune could only be a sign of displeasure, whereas here the Father who sends trouble corrects in love.

debates: Does the command require tithes or free giving? Keil and Delitzsch treat it as a general ethical expression older than the law and note that the technical terms are absent; Clarke keeps a fixed portion of all produce owing; Gill asks only what can prudently be spared in proportion to the estate.
Who is addressed as my son? Gill argues from the New Testament quotation that it is not a son of Solomon nor a pupil but every child of God in every age.

How far has the doctrine of suffering moved? Ellicott sees a wonderful advance beyond the Pentateuch, where misfortune could only signify displeasure; Keil and Delitzsch make the two verses the problem and the solution of the book of Job; Gill uses the passage to answer the objection raised by the promise of plenty.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch find a small paradox in the wording, since the verb for honour means to make heavy while the noun for wealth means lightness in the sense of opulence.
Clarke warns that a man who kicks against the pricks wounds his own soul, and that God will either end him or mend him.
Clarke observes that the Septuagint rendering of the last clause is quoted word for word by the apostle.
themes: substance that is honestly a man’s own
a portion that sanctifies the rest
giving as the way to increase
correction as a school
a father who corrects in love

13.pericope_label: Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding. For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold. She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her. Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and honour. Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her

schools.summary: Henry asks what we actually get by wisdom once it is found, the prospect of advantage being the spring and spur of industry, and answers that to find it is first to get it: to derive it from God, drawing it with the bucket of prayer from the fountain of all wisdom; to take pains for it as a man draws ore out of a mine, putting the more strength to it when it does not come easily; to improve in it, making five talents ten; and to do good with it, drawing from the stock as wine from the vessel and communicating things new and old to others.

Gill takes wisdom throughout the passage to be Christ himself, so that finding him supposes a seeking that arises not from nature but from grace; the believer is a spiritual merchant and faith a trading with and for Christ, in which a man parts with sinful pleasures, his own righteousness, friends set in competition and even life, while silver is inferior because a man may have abundance of it and lose his soul and is never satisfied with it, whereas he who has Christ has enough. On the precious stones he records the Targum and Septuagint rendering them simply precious stones and one Latin version as all riches, and notes the gradation from silver to fine gold to jewels. He pictures wisdom as a queen holding length of days where a sceptre would be and riches and honour where the globe would be, recalls that the king who asked for wisdom received long life and riches with it, fills her ways with the successive acts by which Christ saved his people, and hears in the tree of life an allusion to the tree in the garden.

Clarke works the trading metaphor from the word itself, the traffic carried through countries and provinces on the backs of camels, from a root meaning to go about, the gain being the produce left after all expenses are paid, and compares the mines where a slave won his liberty by finding a diamond of so many carats, while the man who finds wisdom obtains the liberty of the Gospel and is adopted as an heir. He takes the stone principally for pearls though it may cover precious stones generally, reports that one scholar took the root, which means to look or behold, for the loadstone, and suggests that a ruby may be named from the cutting that gives it different faces. He denies any distinction between the two hands, since they are alike full of the choicest benefits, but grants that a wicked man shortens his days by excess as a righteous man lengthens his by temperance; and on the tree of life he holds it probable enough that the fruit of the tree in the garden might have repaired the wastes of nature continually and prevented death for ever. Wesley says finding supposes diligent searching, makes peace a blessed tranquillity of mind and conscience, and calls the tree a pledge of everlasting life and the only restorer of the life we lost by sin.

Keil and Delitzsch argue for corals from the name itself, built on the idea of shooting forth after the manner of plants so that it covers a branch and whatever multiplies branch-like, and from the redness attributed to them elsewhere in contrast with the whiteness of snow and milk, allowing that the sense may have become generalized in practice, since later authorities render pearls. They weigh the two hands, length of days being the chief good and belonging in the right while riches and honour are the addition, goods which do not condition life but, received from wisdom, elevate its happiness. They define the pleasant ways as those on which a man obtains what agrees with the inner and the outer man, and insist the paths are not paths of peace but peace itself, since wisdom brings well-being on all sides and a deep inward satisfaction; and they take the tree of life from the history of paradise. Ellicott calls the Hebrew of the stone doubtful, agrees the colour was red, thinks coral probable and pearls unlikely, calls peace the highest reward held out in the New Testament for a life of thankful dependence on God, and notes that the tree of life is mentioned only in this book and one other.

debates: What stone is meant? Keil and Delitzsch argue for corals from the root and from the redness attributed to them elsewhere, and Ellicott agrees, calling pearls unlikely; Clarke holds the word principally means pearls; Gill reports the versions that generalize it to precious stones or simply riches.

Do the two hands mean different things? Keil and Delitzsch make the right the chief good and the left an addition that does not condition life; Clarke denies that anything is to be understood by the right hand in preference to the left.

Are her paths paths of peace, or peace itself? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the genitive and make the paths themselves peace; Ellicott and Wesley read peace as the reward and the inward tranquillity that follows.
outliers: Clarke compares the mines, where a slave won his liberty by finding a diamond of a given weight, with the greater prize of the man who finds wisdom.

Keil and Delitzsch quote an older commentator that the right hand signifies knowledge of divine things, from which immortal life arises, and the left knowledge of human things, from which glory and abundance are born.
Clarke reports that one scholar took the root, meaning to look or behold, for the loadstone, and closes his note on the incomparable value of wisdom by asking who believes it.
themes: wisdom drawn like ore from a mine
faith as a merchandise
coral, pearl or ruby
a queen with both hands full
paths that are themselves peace
the tree of the garden

19.pericope_label: The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens. By his knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew. My son, let not them depart from thine eyes: keep sound wisdom and discretion: so shall they be life unto thy soul, and grace to thy neck. Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely, and thy foot shall not stumble. When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet

schools.summary: Henry asks that the rules of religion be kept always in view and always at heart, since a man learning to write keeps his eye on the copy and the words of wisdom are to be looked at the same way, while the heart is the treasury in which they are stored, this being wealth worth keeping; and he makes wisdom life to the soul in that it quickens a man when he begins to be slothful and revives him when he droops under trouble.

Gill takes the wisdom by which the earth was founded to be the essential Wisdom of God, the Son, not used as an instrument but an efficient cause with the Father, and cites a Targum reading by wisdom God created. He understands the depths as the source of fountains and rivers and the cavity that holds the sea, and reports that some apply the words to the flood and others to the dividing of the sea when Israel came out of Egypt. On the exhortation he insists that what is to be kept in view is not the works done by Wisdom but wisdom itself, which is one of the names of Christ, and takes the promised life to be Christ himself, the Gospel being the means of reviving drooping saints. The confidence he spells out at bedtime: a man who has committed himself to a faithful Creator is not afraid of thieves, of fire consuming his dwelling, or of nocturnal apparitions, nor is he surprised out of sleep or terrified in it by anxious cares and distressing dreams.

Clarke takes wisdom here in what he calls its proper acceptation, the knowledge and skill manifested in the composition of the earth and the economy of the heavens, holding that God established the order as well as the essence of things so that though they vary in position they never change their places or properties. He credits God with determining how to break up the fountains of the great deep, appointing the fissures through which springs rise, and exhaling and precipitating the vapours, and remarks that the wisest of men ascribes to God the effects we suppose to spring from natural causes. From the two nouns of the exhortation he draws a creed, that to acknowledge God as the author of all good is the essence of a godly man’s belief and to resolve to act by his direction is the purpose that follows. On the sleep he observes that most people are afraid of it lest they never wake, knowing themselves neither innocent nor pardoned, whereas those who know God is their keeper lie down confident and sleep sweetly, undisturbed by foreboding and evil dreams. Wesley leaves the wisdom of creation open, either Christ or that divine perfection which is the fountain of wisdom in man, reads the eyes as the eyes of the mind, and glosses the grace to the neck as a beautiful chain or ornament.

Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading that makes the breaking up of the depths a division of the waters above the firmament from those below, since the verb is used of water bursting forth from the bowels of the earth; the sense is the overflowing of the ground for cultivation and irrigation, the depths being its internal water stores, while the second clause concerns the waters above, the word for clouds naming the uppermost thin stratum of air. They call the return from creation to exhortation characteristic, since the writer speaks of wisdom only with an ethical intention, and identify the things to be kept as wisdom, understanding and knowledge, which belong to God and become the possession of those who aim at them; and they read the promise as larger than safety, wisdom making its possessor confident in God in every situation of life. Ellicott calls the founding of the earth by wisdom anticipatory of a doctrine stated in the New Testament, notes that a further advance toward the personality of the Creator comes later in this book, renders the verb of the depths as burst forth, and observes that dew matters greatly where for months together there is no rain.

debates: Whose wisdom founded the earth? Gill and Ellicott read it of the Son, Ellicott calling the verse anticipatory of a New Testament doctrine; Clarke takes it in its proper acceptation as the knowledge and skill God showed in creation; Wesley leaves both open.

What does the breaking up of the depths mean? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the sense of dividing the waters and read water bursting from the interior of the earth for irrigation; Gill and Clarke both hear the flood in it, Gill adding the dividing of the sea at the exodus.

Is the security bodily or spiritual? Gill and Clarke both take the promise down to the bedroom, thieves and fire and bad dreams; Keil and Delitzsch make it confidence in God in every situation; Henry makes it a quickening of the soul.
outliers: Clarke remarks that the wisest of men ascribes to God himself the effects we suppose to spring from natural causes.
Clarke notes that most people fear sleep because they know themselves neither innocent nor pardoned.
Ellicott observes that dew is of great importance in countries where for months together there is no rain.
themes: the earth founded by wisdom
depths that burst from within
a copy kept before the eye
a creed drawn from two nouns
sleep without foreboding

25.pericope_label: Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it cometh. For the Lord shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken. Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee. Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee. Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm. Envy thou not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways

schools.summary: Henry holds that true wisdom lies in the discharge of our duty toward man as well as toward God, in honesty as well as piety, and traces the withholding of good either to want of love for the poor or to too much love of money. A man who has disabled himself by extravagance is at fault; one whom God has disabled should grieve less that he is straitened in his own comforts than that he has nothing left to give. The excuse of a more convenient season he answers by the plain fact that no one is sure of living until tomorrow.

Gill takes the sudden fear of anything terrible that comes unawares or of rumours that danger is near, and answers that a man should think himself safe under the care of the keeper of Israel, who neither slumbers nor sleeps; he also reports the rendering that the Lord shall be in thy confidence, supporting it so that a man does not cast it away. Under the good that is due he lists honour, reverence and tribute to civil magistrates and just payment of debts to creditors as well as alms to the poor, which he thinks chiefly meant. He prefers the ploughing sense of the next warning, turning up the heart to find evil against a neighbour as the earth is turned by the plough, when a good man should devise all the good he can; divides striving into words, wrangling contentiously over mere trifles, and deeds, lawsuits brought on nothing worth litigating; and describes the oppressor as one who gets wealth by injustice, rapine and violence, whose place is not to be envied since his end will be bad.

Clarke renders the phrase from the lords of it and identifies those owners as the poor, making the rich man a steward given substance that he may divide it, so that the poor own every farthing he can spare beyond his own support; were it a civil case the law would take him by the throat and lay him up in prison, but here God alone judges, and judgment without mercy awaits the man who has shown none. He urges haste because death may take the giver or the asker before the morrow, warns against a litigious spirit and too nice a sense of honour, asking why a man should contend where no harm has been done when others might contend with him on the same terms, and closes the envy warning with the observation that power is bewitching, every man desiring it while all hate tyrants, though if all had power the greater part would be tyrants themselves. Wesley explains the fear as sudden because unexpected evils are the most frightful and takes fear for the evils feared, widens the good to be given past money to counsel, comfort, reproof and the good things of the present life and the recipients to all men by the great and sovereign law of love, notes that the neighbour dwells securely because he relies on your integrity, and makes the envy an envy of the oppressor’s impunity and success.

Keil and Delitzsch organize the precepts as illustrations of neighbourly love, readiness to serve first, then harmlessness, then peaceableness, and finally a warning against fellowship with the loveless. On devising evil they weigh a verb that means to cut into, used of the smith and the carpenter but just as commonly of ploughing, so that the phrase may mean either to fabricate evil or to plough it, and note that the old versions divide between the neutral sense of contriving and the Greek sense of fabricating. On striving they hold that contending with any man without sufficient reason ought to be abandoned, since no such reason exists where he has inflicted no evil; and on the last warning they observe that jealousy and envy are inseparable in the word used. Ellicott glosses the desolation of the wicked as the storm which overwhelms them, and identifies those to whom good is due as the poor and needy, urging that we are not absolute owners but stewards of the manifold grace of God, so that the friends made by our liberality may welcome us when we fail.

debates: Who are they to whom good is due? Clarke calls the poor the lords or right owners of the rich man’s surplus and Ellicott agrees, making the giver a steward; Wesley extends the debt to all men by the law of love; Gill keeps magistrates and creditors in the list beside the poor.

Is the evil devised or ploughed? Keil and Delitzsch set out both senses of the verb and note that the versions divide; Gill takes the ploughing image and makes it the turning up of the heart to find evil.

What removes the ground of a quarrel? Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke agree that no sufficient reason exists where a man has done no harm, Clarke adding that the litigant invites the same treatment from others.
outliers: Clarke says that were the withholding of the poor a civil case the law would take the rich man by the throat and lay him up in prison, but here God alone judges.
Clarke closes on the bewitching quality of power, that every man desires it and all hate tyrants, and asks whether, if all had power, the greater part would not be tyrants.
Gill reports a rendering by which the Lord is in a man’s confidence, supporting it so that he does not cast it away.
themes: safety under a keeper who never sleeps
the poor as the true owners
a duty that cannot wait for tomorrow
evil ploughed rather than devised
a quarrel without a cause
the oppressor who is not to be envied

32.pericope_label: For the froward is abomination to the Lord: but his secret is with the righteous. The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but he blesseth the habitation of the just. Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly. The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools

schools.summary: Gill takes the froward as one perverse in words and actions, cites an Arabic version rendering him simply a transgressor of the law, and says he is not merely abominable in God’s sight but an abomination itself. He keeps the curse legal, the wicked man being under the curse of the law so that his house, his substance and his very blessings are curses and a plentiful estate may end in penury, and reports a reading that makes it the curse of want. On the scorners he describes those who make a mock at sin and a jest of religion, notes that the Greek version followed by two apostles renders the clause he resisteth the proud, and reports a scholar who defends that version as agreeable both to the Hebrew and to the Jewish writers, one of whom explains the scorners as men who will not look upon the divine Being but go on boldly in sin as though there were no God, another as those who exalt themselves. He identifies the wise with the just and lowly already named, and defines the wisdom as neither natural nor civil nor merely notional but a wisdom unto salvation, in which a man knows the sinfulness of his nature, his inability to do good and his want of a righteousness to justify him.

Clarke reads the secret concretely as a secret assembly where godly people meet and God dwells, and makes the two dwellings a matter of company, since no godly people meet in the house of the wicked and God is never an inmate there, while he counts the habitation of the just his own temple, worshipped in spirit and in truth. He gives the Greek line about resisting the proud and notes that two apostles quote it exactly as it stands there, changing only which divine name is used; and he grounds the inheritance of glory in family, the wise man being a child of the heavenly household with heaven for his portion, while fools have ignominy for their exaltation, many of them exalted to the gibbet and gallows. Wesley concludes that the froward must sooner or later be miserable while the righteous are God’s friends, to whom he imparts favours and comforts that other men are strangers to, and notes that the curse on the house falls on the posterity as well as on the person.

Keil and Delitzsch insist that neither curse nor blessing is a matter of external goods, the centre of the curse being a continuous disquiet of conscience and that of the blessing the happy consciousness that God is with us, a rest of soul certain of his grace and goodness; they note that the poetic word for the dwelling means a place of settlement and may be borrowed from nomad life, since it specially denotes pasture-ground. On the scorners they resist the common rendering that makes the first clause a condition and the second its consequence, since the one fact is not the consequence but the reverse of the other and the connecting word in such antitheses generally means on the other hand, while several old versions pass over the particle and one translator makes it an asseveration the word cannot bear. On the last verse they refuse the rendering that shame sweeps fools away, since the verb means to raise something high, and prefer that shame exalts them, in the sense that they owe their celebrity to it as warning examples. Ellicott takes the secret of the Lord as confidential intercourse, compares the promise that Father and Son will make their abode with the believer, traces the word for habitation to pasture or sheepfold as a relic of nomad life, renders the scorner clause although he scorns the scorners yet to the lowly he giveth grace, and reads it as another form of the earlier teaching that offers of mercy rejected are in time withdrawn.

debates: Is the curse material or inward? Keil and Delitzsch put its centre in a continuous disquiet of conscience and the blessing in the consciousness that God is with us; Gill keeps it legal and concrete, a plentiful estate reduced to penury; Wesley extends it to the posterity.

How should the scorner clause be construed? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the conditional reading and make the two facts the reverse of each other; Ellicott renders it although he scorns the scorners, yet to the lowly he giveth grace; Gill and Clarke follow the Greek that the apostles quote, he resisteth the proud.

What does shame do to fools? Keil and Delitzsch deny that it sweeps them away, since the verb means to raise up, and read it as exalting them into warning examples; Ellicott agrees that they are noticeable only as examples to be shunned; Clarke keeps it plainer, ignominy for their exaltation.
outliers: Ellicott reports that some find a contrast between the well-built house of the wicked and the slight cottage of the humble just man, no better than a shepherd’s hut.
Clarke reads the secret of the Lord as a secret assembly, where godly people meet and God dwells, and calls the house of the just his own temple.
Clarke observes that many of the fools spoken of here are exalted to the gibbet and gallows.
themes: a man who is himself an abomination
a curse felt in the conscience
a dwelling that recalls the sheepfold
the Greek that the apostles quote
shame that raises fools into examples
